First reasoned review: 0816a08e655c, 19b7d3b29ea8, 7d7db1f651fc
================================================================

Verdicts and identification
---------------------------

0816a08e655c: MALICIOUS. C# CloudTasks OneDrive task agent source,
byte-identical to testdata/hostile/cloud-managed-tasking/direct-results.cs.
Main reads DRIVE_TOKEN for Bearer authentication, lists Graph drive root
children, and repeats the dispatch every 30 seconds. The .module branch
downloads assembly bytes, loads them with Assembly.Load, resolves a reflected
method, invokes it with argv and PUTs its return value. The .collect branch
downloads a local path, reads that file, and PUTs those same bytes. The
.receive branch splits an HTTP descriptor: element zero selects the remote
item, element one supplies the local write destination. It then PUTs an OK
status. There is no restriction to an application-owned local directory.

19b7d3b29ea8: MALICIOUS. C# CloudTasks source, byte-identical to the existing
different-body.cs fixture. Its hex-looking suffixes select the same assembly
execution/result-return and remote-file-deployment operations. Its middle
branch reads the remotely supplied local filename but uploads UTF-8 bytes
of "fixed report". The read data is unused. File acquisition is supported;
file-content exfiltration in that branch is not. The existing file-exfiltration
rule correctly does not fire here and was not weakened or duplicated.

The balance for both C# sources is an unrestricted remote code/file-control
agent: cloud-controlled assembly execution, result return, arbitrary local
file reads and remote-selected file writes. Authorized administration and
research are possible deployment contexts, but are not established by these
sources. They are source specimens, not recovered deployed implants or proof
of a particular malware family or intrusion. Token ownership, installation,
operator authorization and the fetched assemblies are unknown. No shell
execution is inferred from a reflected method's name. Environment-token use
is authentication, not credential theft. A polling loop is not durable
persistence. No bootkit, initial-access method, encryption or anti-analysis
behavior is inferred.

7d7db1f651fc: BENIGN. craft-native 0.0.340, the Craft TypeScript/native-app
SDK. A fresh forager fetch of pkg:npm/craft-native@0.0.340 from npm has the
same complete SHA-256 as the supplied tarball. The manifest points to
craft-native/craft, packages/typescript; runtime dependencies are empty.
The top-level manifest has a prepublishOnly build and no install-time hook.
Provenance and artifact are saved together under scratch/fallout-review/
provenance/npm/. This comparison establishes release identity, not a general
trust guarantee for all versions or future fetched code.

The bundle exports library APIs; the CLI dispatches user-selected build,
package, device, signing and development-server operations. CraftApp.show
resolves the configured/installed native runtime and spawns it with window
configuration arguments. The process API exposes an explicit exec wrapper;
it does not start a shell connected to a controller when imported. Cleanup
targets owned temporary directories and dead-process leftovers.

AutoUpdater fetches a configured manifest, streams the selected download into
a file while hashing it, and checks the expected digest before installation.
It can verify a configured public-key signature. The macOS path verifies
codesign and, by default, Gatekeeper/notarization, checks an optional Team ID,
then removes quarantine and swaps the application bundle. Those permission,
execution, download, cryptographic and quarantine capabilities remain visible.
They are not evidence of malware or a Gatekeeper bypass on this artifact.

The three ML-hostile Swift members were traced separately:

* CraftApp.swift implements the application/WebKit bridge, device permissions,
  app-origin checks, native controls, contacts, camera/audio and local storage.
  Its sensitive native surface is an SDK feature rather than an autonomous
  harvesting loop. The trusted-origin decision is shared by bridge handlers.
* CraftNativeFiles.swift uses system file/photo/video pickers, writes picked
  media into app-owned temporary storage, and constructs multipart files.
  owned() resolves symlinks and requires a regular file under that owned root.
  NativeActions hands that multipart file to URLSession.uploadTask; download
  tasks save requested media. NWPathMonitor.start monitors connectivity and
  is not an NWConnection socket start. Cache cleanup concerns owned media.
* CraftCrashReporter.swift starts only with configured crashReporting and a
  nonempty key. It records application crashes/hangs/JavaScript errors, queues
  reports locally and posts them to the configured host or bughq.org. Its
  vm_read_overwrite calls use mach_task_self_ to recover this process's crash
  frames/messages, rather than reading another application's secrets.

The ESM/CommonJS/CLI output is a normal readable bundle, not an obscured
execution stage. Recovered Unicode escapes are presentation/error text and
input-validation characters; URL-decoded quoting belongs to multipart
headers. Base64 and crypto paths provide data/attachment operations. The
high-entropy media member is an MP4 test asset. Static review found no
supported theft, spying, destructive operation, backdoor or user deception.
An embedding application's configuration and eventual use of these APIs are
unknown. The benign verdict rests on traced SDK behavior and provenance,
rather than its zero hostile/suspicious trait count.

Detection changes
-----------------

1. Add an adjacent-statement C# matcher binding GetStringAsync's result to
   File.ReadAllBytes' path. Add a separate collection objective that requires
   the established cloud code/result task channel as well as that bound read.
   This covers the fixed-report variant without claiming file exfiltration.
   Fixed paths, intervening reassignment and inert comments do not satisfy it.
2. Move the unchanged start(queue:) source matcher from socket/state-connect
   to source call-syntax metadata. The old rule never established the receiver
   type. Preserve the exact reverse-shell consumer with the new ID; its
   independent NWConnection construction, send/receive and shell/stdio legs
   still fire on the repository's real Swift reverse-shell fixture.
3. Add notable, parsed-call detections for NWPathMonitor construction,
   URLSession downloadTask/uploadTask and Mach virtual-memory reads. They
   describe capabilities without inventing surveillance or another process.
4. Correct chmod literal-target matching to require a command boundary.
   The former matcher treated "or chmod +x the file directly" in both Craft
   entry-point error messages as a command targeting "the". Those two notable
   member findings disappear. Actual CI chmod commands and permission-changing
   calls remain. Four control-file losses are also unsupported matches: prose
   in a JSON case description, the prose near miss, and two shell comments
   where whitespace crossed a newline and consumed wget/curl as the supposed
   chmod target. All hostile/suspicious control findings are retained.
5. Rename Assembly.Load's identifier-argument observation, keeping its matcher,
   scope and severity. The prior buffer/bytes claim was unsupported because
   the argument can instead hold an assembly-name string; the existing
   string-assembly-name.cs fixture demonstrates this. Update seven consumer
   YAML files without changing their conditions.
6. Consolidate the two curl -F file-attachment observations into the canonical
   upload trait and update both exact consumers. They described the same
   operation with differing scope/length bounds. Retain the longer quoted
   shell form, Unix scope and non-shell/binary coverage. Legitimate Omarchy
   uploads also retain the neutral capability, as the former shell detector
   already did. File-free forms do not satisfy the attachment matcher. The
   archive-upload, AppleScript and hostile PowerShell positives retain all
   attack findings. This is semantic deduplication, not a severity reduction.

Consumers and scope
-------------------

Exact and ancestor references were inspected, including port-probe consumers
of socket/state-connect, upload-directory consumers, the Swift stream-bridge,
the archive/exploit upload consumers, and all Assembly.Load rename consumers.
The source queue-call matcher keeps its original scope and evidence; the
port-probe rule is C/C++ scoped. The upload merger removes duplicate evidence
for one transfer operation. No package-specific exception was added. No
finding in this batch originated in a fetched runtime dependency.

Verification and limitations
----------------------------

atomscan and cleave facts were run on every original. Facts were also dumped
for the main bundles, Android builder, native actions and the three flagged
Swift sources. Source, decoded text, call records, task branches and actual
write/upload bodies were inspected. C# and some embedded-source flow graphs
have recorded limitations; the new C# detector uses bound adjacent AST nodes.
The samples were not executed and no cloud token or task endpoint was used.

The reproducible command uses --follow=none, --analyze local, --mode slow and
--no-update. Both clean before and after scans complete for every original.
The before replay uses a pristine HEAD trait snapshot in scratch; its trait
fingerprint, every original finding and all three classifier probabilities
exactly reproduce the initial pre-edit scans.

check.py compares 32 source controls, 22 chmod control analyses and four curl
form analyses. The existing cloud-task regression script also passes all 24
cases after the Assembly.Load rename. Before/after comparisons include all
224 analyzed Craft units, including archive members and extracted workflow
steps. review.json records the exact changes and only intentional losses.
No supported attack finding or severity is lost after canonical-ID mapping.
The new collection objective's computed precision is 5.9, above the 3.5
hostile authoring threshold; its factual source and tasking requirements
were separately checked with positive and near-miss controls.

                      hostile before/after  suspicious before/after
direct-results.cs              5 / 6                 3 / 3
different-body.cs              6 / 7                 3 / 3
craft-native 0.0.340            0 / 0                 0 / 0

The C# variants cover remote managed-code tasking, invocation-result return,
file deployment and remote-selected acquisition; direct-results additionally
has the bound file-content upload. No additional security-relevant detection
gap was identified in these sources.
The malicious trait-count guidance is met by distinct behaviors across C2,
collection and, for the direct variant, exfiltration; accurate older findings
were not removed to fit a numeric range.

All three ML verdicts remain HOSTILE. Craft is a remaining classifier false
positive: probability 1.0 is inherited from the three native Swift SDK files,
despite zero hostile or suspicious traits. C# probabilities remain above
0.9999 and agree with the review. The installed model additionally warns that
its v18 feature specification predates expected v21; new features are not
fully represented by that model. Neither inaccurate rules nor duplicated
traits were restored to alter its scores.

Exactly one verdict marker is written beside each original sample. The final
required action is make validate; its result is reported in the task response.
